In mathematical notation—specifically when defining intervals on a number line—brackets and parentheses have very specific meanings regarding whether or not the "endpoint" number is included in the set.

Intervals and Inclusion

  • Parentheses $( \text{ or } )$ are non-inclusive. This is called an open interval. It means the set includes every number up to the boundary, but not the boundary number itself.
  • Brackets $[ \text{ or } ]$ are inclusive. This is called a closed interval. It means the set includes the boundary number.

Comparison Table

NotationNameMeaningIncludes Endpoint?
$(a, b)$Open IntervalAll numbers $x$ such that $a < x < b$No
$[a, b]$Closed IntervalAll numbers $x$ such that $a \le x \le b$Yes
$[a, b)$Half-OpenAll numbers $x$ such that $a \le x < b$Only $a$

Real-World Examples

  1. Ages (Non-inclusive): If a contest is for people "between the ages of 18 and 25" and uses parentheses $(18, 25)$, a person who is exactly 18 or exactly 25 would technically be excluded.
  2. Price Ranges (Inclusive): If a store says items are "[$10, $20]," you can expect to find items that cost exactly $10.00 and exactly $20.00.

Infinity $\infty$

Note that Infinity always uses a parenthesis, never a bracket. Because infinity is a concept rather than a specific reachable number, you cannot "include" it in the set.

  • Correct: $[0, \infty)$
  • Incorrect: $[0, \infty]$
